summary: Abu Dardaa and Anas bin Maalik closed their hadith reports with a qualifying phrase, so as not to claim more than the Prophet's exact words.
notes: The OCR joins two reports, and the Muhammad bin Seereen clause is garbled, so it may belong to a separate report. Only one approved theme fits.

summary: Anas bin Maalik narrated few hadith and always added the qualifying phrase. Abu Ja'far Muhammad bin Ali says no Companion was more careful in narrating than Abdullaah bin Umar.
notes: The line opens with 'Rasulullaah said', but the words that follow are Abu Ja'far's. The attribution looks like a transcription error. The text also has no closing quote.

summary: Sha'bi says he sat with Abdullaah bin Umar for a full year and never heard him narrate a hadith from the Prophet.
Imraan bin Husayn says he has memorised many hadith but holds back from narrating them, because some of his companions may differ with him over the wording.
notes: Only one approved theme fits.

summary: Mutarraf reports that Imraan bin Husayn could narrate hadith for two days without repeating one, but refrained because companions confuse the sequence of words. He was exact when quoting the Prophet.
notes: Mutarraf's sahabi status is my inference (a Tabi'i by standard references), not stated in the book.

summary: Suhayb tells Sulaymaan bin Abu Abdullaah that he will never say 'Rasulullaah said' for a hadith, though he will relate what he experienced on the expeditions.
Makhool and Abul Azhar asked Waathila bin Asqa for a hadith in exact words. He replied that they had not mastered the Qur'aan, and that narrators should relate only the meaning.
notes: OCR garbles the short quoted reply ('add a Waawd) or an'), so the exact wording there is uncertain.

summary: Before his death Umar summoned Companions from distant lands, asked what hadith they were spreading, and kept them in Madinah. He also confined Abdullaah bin Mas'ood, Abu Mas'ood and Abu Dardaa there.
notes: Two reports: Ibraheem's account of Umar summoning four Companions, and a second, also related by Ibraheem, of Umar confining three others to Madinah.

summary: Ibn Abu Awfa reports that when asked to narrate hadith, Zaid bin Arqam said he had grown old and forgetful, and that narrating the Prophet's hadith was a serious matter.
notes: 'Ibn Abu Awfa' is matched to Abdullaah bin Abi Awfa by name only, since the text gives no first name. Only one approved theme fits.

summary: Mu'aadh bin Jabal and Abu Dardaa both said that knowledge brings no benefit until it is practised. Anas bin Maalik said the same, that there is no reward for knowledge until it is put into practice.
notes: Joint saying of Mu'aadh and Abu Dardaa, followed by a separate saying of Anas.

summary: Abdur Rahmaan bin Ghanam reports that ten Companions were learning in the Masjid of Quba when the Prophet came and told them to learn.
notes: The text gives only the opening word 'Learn...' and says the rest matches the narration above. The ten unnamed Companions are omitted.

summary: Ali reports that a man asked the Prophet what would be the proof against him for ignorance and what would be the proof against him for knowledge. The Prophet answered knowledge, and then action.
notes: OCR garbles the last reply ('Rasulullaah Seal's reply'). The unnamed man is omitted.

summary: Umar tells people to study the Book of Allaah and practise its teachings, so that they become among its worthy bearers.
notes: The trailing editorial reference to a variant that names Abu Dharr and Abdullaah bin Mas'ood is not counted as people in this narration.

summary: Ali tells people to study and practise, warning that a time will come when most of the truth is rejected. Only the anonymous, aloof people who are the lanterns of knowledge will be saved, and they are not hasty and do not spread immoral behaviour or speech.
Ali warns of people of knowledge whose private lives contradict their public teaching, who boast in their gatherings, and whose actions will not rise to Allaah.
notes: The 'hypocrisy' theme is my reading of the contrast between private and public life.

summary: Ibn Mas'ood urges people to practise what they learn. Abdullaah bin Ukaym and Adi bin Adi relate his warnings that Allaah will question each person about whether they practised their knowledge.
notes: Three reports are joined: Ibn Mas'ood's own words, Ibn Ukaym's account of a speech, and Adi bin Adi's report of further sayings. Adi bin Adi is not in the approved list.

summary: Abu Dardaa said he feared being asked on the Day of Judgement whether he practised his knowledge. He also said that the worst person before Allaah is one whose knowledge does not benefit him.
notes: Several of Abu Dardaa's sayings are joined. OCR breaks the wording in places ('1 am at Your service', 'Did you practise on your'). 'O Uwaymir' is Abu Dardaa's own name, not a second person.

summary: Mu'aadh bin Jabal said that no one will be able to move on the Day of Judgement until he is questioned about four things, including how he practised his knowledge.

Mu'aadh bin Jabal says no reward is given for knowledge until it is practised. Anas bin Maalik adds that true scholars aim to remember and practise, while foolish people aim only to pass knowledge on.
notes: Mu'aadh's saying and Anas's saying are joined. The text ends with stray marks.

summary: Ubay bin Ka'b urges holding fast to the straight path and the Sunnah. He says that moderate deeds done for Allaah's pleasure are better than exertion that goes against the Sunnah, and that deeds should be checked against the way of the Prophets.

Sa'eed bin Musayyib reports Umar's address after returning to Madinah, that the Sunan have been shown and the Faraa'idh ordained. Ibn Mas'ood then taught that every new introduction in the Deen is a bid'ah, and warned against distant hopes that make one forget the Aakhirah.
notes: Umar's address and Ibn Mas'ood's Thursday lecture are two separate reports under one heading.

summary: Ibn Mas'ood says that moderation in the Sunnah is better than striving in bid'ah.
Imraan bin Husayn says the Qur'aan was revealed and the Prophet showed how to live by it, and that people must follow the Companions or they will go astray.

Imraan bin Husayn rebukes a man who would follow only the Qur'aan. He shows that the details of prayer, zakaah and other rules come from the Sunnah, which explains what the Qur'aan states only briefly.
notes: The man he rebukes is unnamed and is omitted.

summary: Ibn Mas'ood urges people to follow the Companions of the Prophet, who had the most righteous hearts, the deepest knowledge and the most upright example in the Ummah.
Hudhayfah urges the Qurraa to fear Allaah and follow those who came before them, warning that whoever turns from their path goes far astray.
notes: 'Hadhrat Hudhayfah' has no patronymic. Matched to Hudhayfah bin Yamaan as the usual referent of this advice, so please confirm. Stray ''' marks at the end are OCR debris.

summary: Mus'ab bin Sa'd reports that his father, Sa'd bin Abi Waqqaas, kept congregational prayer brief but prolonged it when praying alone. He told his son that the Companions are the leaders to be followed.
Ibn Mas'ood says to follow and not introduce new ways, because the Prophet and the Companions have already laid the path.
notes: The opening line repeats the heading. Abu Bakr and Umar appear in the text only in that heading phrase, so they are listed as mentioned.

summary: Ibn Mas'ood says that loving Abu Bakr and Umar and acknowledging their worth is an integral part of the Sunnah.

Ali warns against imitating living people, since a person may change course for better or worse and die in that state. He says that if one must follow someone, it should be those who died as practising believers.
When Ibn Mas'ood learned that a group in the Masjid was performing dhikr in set counts led by one man, he confronted them, called it a wrong bid'ah, and had them disperse.
notes: Two versions of one incident. Ma'dad and Amr bin Utba speak in both. Their names are OCR-garbled and they are not in the approved list.

summary: Ibn Mas'ood confronts groups in the Masjid of Kufa and between Maghrib and Isha, saying they have strayed very quickly while the Companions are still alive. Abu Moosa Ash'ari brings him word of the dhikr group.
notes: Three accounts run together: the Kufa visit, the Abu Moosa episode, and Amr Ibn Salamah's account of the walk to the Masjid.

summary: Abdullaah bin Zubayr finds his son Aamir sitting with people who fall unconscious in dhikr, and tells him never to sit with them again, since the Companions did not behave like this.
notes: Begins mid-sentence, so the opening is missing. The text gives Aamir as (RA), but the approved list marks this Aamir as not a Sahabi. I followed the approved list. The heading contains a stray OCR number ('292.').

summary: Sila bin Haarith Ghifaari rebukes Anz Nujaybi, who was telling stories in the Masjid, saying the Companions had scarcely left the Prophet's time and that such innovations should not appear among them yet.

people.name: Abu Saalih Sa'eed bin Abdur Rahmaan

notes: Abu Saalih is not matched to the approved 'abu-saalih' entry, which may be a different person.

summary: Amr bin Zuraarah says that while he was relating stories in the Masjid, Ibn Mas'ood called it a misleading bid'ah, and everyone around him dispersed.

Ibn Shihaab reports Umar's sermon that accurate opinions came only from the Prophet, whom Allaah guided. Sadaqah bin Abu Abdullaah reports Umar's warning that those who follow personal opinion are enemies of the Sunnah.
notes: Ibn Shihaab's report and Sadaqah's report are separate. A variant adds a Qur'aan quotation (Surah Najm, verse 28). Ibn Shihaab's report is OCR-garbled.

summary: Umar says the Sunnah is what Allaah and His Rasool have determined. When asked whether Allaah guided him in his judgements, he said that guidance was a speciality of the Prophet.
notes: The first sentence is cut off ('never make your mistaken opinion a'). A second report from Amr bin Dinaar follows it.

summary: Sha'bi relates Ibn Mas'ood's warning against asking for opinions and judging one matter by another, and his saying that 'Allaah knows best' is a third of knowledge. Ibn Mas'ood also foresaw that after the Ulema die, people would destroy Islaam by personal opinion.
notes: Two sayings are joined: the warning against 'what is your opinion', and a later saying about the death of the Ulema.

summary: Ibn Abbaas says the basis of Islaam is the Book of Allaah and the Sunnah. A Companion, reported through Ataa from his father, says he is too shy before his Rabb to give a personal opinion on matters affecting the Ummah.
notes: Ataa's report is cut off mid-sentence. The unnamed Companion is omitted. Ataa is not matched to an approved entry, since the text gives no patronymic.

summary: Mu'aadh bin Jabal tells how the Prophet, sending him to Yemen, asked how he would judge. He answered by the Book of Allaah, then the Sunnah, then ijtihaad without neglecting diligence, and the Prophet approved.
notes: The trailing Tabraani and Haythami references are editorial and are not counted.
